findings.title: The document specifies a reusable metrology record extension but no load-bearing record schema
findings.description: The architecture commits to two new `record_type` values as optional sibling payloads on `MetrologyRecord`, yet it never states the payload fields, identity keys, comparability keys, or absence representation. That is the core contract for every downstream consumer: 420 must read snapshots and normalized review findings, 440 must read the baseline, and the rollup must compare snapshots over time. The current `MetrologyRecord` in `src/squadron/metrology/models.py` has optional siblings such as `audit_run` and `audit_noise_floor`; adding `snapshot` and `review_finding` without a specified shape makes “no schema migration” a statement about the envelope rather than about the data. At minimum the architecture must fix the snapshot identity (`ProjectId`, commit SHA, language/tool identity, rule-set identity, exclusions, dirty marker), the normalized-finding identity (`ProjectId`, reviewed SHA, slice where known, source category, mapping method), and the shape of “absent with reason.” The keystone slice cannot be designed without these choices.

findings.title: The review-category contract cannot be satisfied by the current code-review template
findings.description: The architecture requires that “review templates emit categories from the same closed vocabulary” and that ingest be deterministic, with “the model’s raw string kept beside it” and `other` as fallback. The shipped `src/squadron/data/templates/code.yaml` finding contract contains only `severity`, `location`, and title/description — there is no `category:` tag at all. The parser in `src/squadron/review/parsers.py` reads a free-form `category:` tag only when the model emits one, and `ReviewResult.structured_findings` substitutes `"uncategorized"` when it is absent. This is not a one-line template change: the write path must add a closed-vocabulary category field to the template contract, the parser must validate it, persistence must retain raw and normalized values, and the existing findings-addressed matcher consumes `category` as a free string for identity matching. The document treats write-time categorization as a small write-path change and defers all impact to the normalization slice, understating the coupling to the existing review and 180-series finding matcher.

findings.title: “One snapshot per commit” is incompatible with the stated multi-metric, per-language model
findings.description: The Envisioned State says the command “selects a language adapter for each language present” and “writes one snapshot record per commit,” while the Architectural Principles say the record identifies “the project, commit, language, tool versions, rule set and exclusions.” Those are different grains. A repository with Python and TypeScript has one commit but two language adapters, potentially two tool identities, two rule sets, and two exclusion sets. One record per commit cannot carry a single language/tool/exclusion identity without either collapsing distinct measurements into one record or forcing a multi-valued structure that the comparability rule does not define. The architecture must fix whether the snapshot is per `(commit, language)` — and the store identity accordingly — or per commit with a per-language measurement list, and must define how a report compares a commit whose language set changed.

findings.title: The “project’s own config” for limits, rule sets, and exclusions has no defined location or precedence
findings.description: Three load-bearing inputs are said to come from “project config”: file/function limits, lint/type rule sets, and exclusions. The design goal “without editing the project’s config files” suggests a separate squadron-side configuration, while “the project’s own configured rules” suggests the brownfield repository’s existing config. No file format, key namespace, lookup order, or precedence between the two is given. This matters concretely: squadron’s own rules are stated in prose in `CLAUDE.md`/review rules and its ruff/pyright config lives in `pyproject.toml`, while `src/squadron/config/keys.py` shows squadron config keys are registered centrally and read through `get_config`; an unregistered key raises `KeyError`. Brownfield projects may have no squadron config at all and may express exclusions in many different tool-native formats. “Effective exclusion set” and “named rule set” cannot be recorded without a defined resolution procedure and a content identity for the resolved rule set.

findings.title: The adapter contract defers the hardest semantics to slice design
findings.description: The architecture says the adapter contract “has to define each metric well enough that adapters agree,” but the document does not define what each metric means. Cyclomatic complexity, duplication window/unit, function-length counting rules, lint-count denominator, type-error scope, and coverage denominator are precisely the semantics that determine whether two adapters agree and whether two snapshots are comparable. Deferring this to the keystone slice means the keystone slice’s first task is to invent the semantics, which is architecture work disguised as implementation. A metric-definition section — at minimum per metric: unit of measurement, counting rule, denominator/none, treatment of generated/vendor code, and the identity that invalidates comparison — should be fixed before the first adapter is designed. Otherwise the first Python adapter will define the contract implicitly and the second language adapter will discover that the contract was Python-shaped.

findings.title: Slice attribution is a correctness prerequisite for a headline capability, but it is deferred to a slice decision
findings.description: Per-slice rollup is one of the four advertised capabilities and the stated before/after model for a slice. The document says the mapping source “is a slice decision” while only forbidding commit-message guessing. The existing repository already contains the structural resolver `resolve_slice_diff_range` in `src/squadron/review/git_utils.py`, which handles branch/reflog/merge-commit cases and raises `DiffRangeUnresolvedError` rather than guessing; the architecture neither names that reusable surface nor states the chosen attribution identity. Without a fixed attribution rule, the snapshot record cannot be joined to a slice, and the “per-slice” report cannot be designed at all. Fix commits landing directly on the target and brownfield history with no slices also need an explicit outcome, not silence.

findings.title: The baseline command has no defined contract with the existing capability probe
findings.description: The architecture says 440’s capability probe consumes the adoption baseline and that CF “offers this at handoff through 440’s capability probe.” The agreed cross-repo contract in `project-documents/user/reference/capability-probe-contract.md` already fixes `probe_version: 1` with a single `baseline.available` boolean, and it explicitly says the probe itself is not built yet. This document introduces a materially richer notion of baseline — snapshot plus audit baseline with noise floor — but never states how `baseline.available` is computed, whether it means “the command exists,” “the command can run for this project,” or “a baseline already exists for this project,” nor whether probing may trigger the expensive four-run LLM campaign. A boolean cannot express “baseline exists but was taken under a different audit prompt hash/model.” The architecture must align its baseline notion with the versioned probe contract, including whether the probe gains fields (which requires a `probe_version` bump) or whether baseline availability remains an intentionally coarse signal.

findings.title: Static-metric comparability is asserted but the record does not carry enough identity to enforce it
findings.description: The Architectural Principles require that reports “refuse to diff across a tool change without flagging it,” and the Design Goals require snapshots to identify “tool versions, rule set and exclusions.” Tool versions alone are insufficient for the comparability rule as stated: a changed lint configuration, a changed exclusion set, or a changed project limit changes the measurement even when the tool binary is unchanged. The document mentions naming the rule set and recording the effective exclusion set, but it does not say these are part of the comparability key, nor does it define whether a change in the project-declared length limits invalidates comparison of violation counts (it plainly must, since “violations against limits” is the measured number). The report behavior must be specified per metric, not only per tool version.

findings.title: Snapshot execution failure handling is materially weaker than the audit harness precedent it claims to reuse
findings.description: For a pipeline-attached snapshot, the document requires that a failed snapshot never fail the pipeline step but be “logged and recorded as absent.” For the interactive path there is no failure policy at all: a missing tool, a non-zero analyzer exit, a timeout, a partially written output, or an unreadable project are all “absent with a reason,” but the document does not distinguish “tool unavailable” from “tool ran and found violations” from “tool ran and crashed.” Those are materially different measurements, and the “absent is not zero” rule alone does not say how a crash is represented. The 323 audit slice already established a strong precedent — all-or-nothing persistence, per-mode detection, observable WARNING/ERROR signals, pre-flight checks before spend — and this component should specify the analogous policy rather than leaving the snapshot path to “absent with a reason.” Otherwise a crashed analyzer can be recorded indistinguishably from an analyzer that found nothing.

findings.title: Coverage is in the advertised snapshot scope but its execution model is deferred to a slice decision with a security boundary
findings.description: The Static Snapshot capability lists “coverage where tests run” as a delivered metric, while the Technical Considerations leave open whether the snapshot ever installs dependencies or runs project tests. These are not equivalent implementations. The first executes untrusted project code in the operator’s environment; the second only reads an existing report. The architecture acknowledges “real security and environment cost” but then treats the choice as a slice decision, which means the keystone slice can ship with either behavior and every downstream consumer (420 scoring, 440 baseline) inherits it. This is a security-boundary decision with a fixed direction needed now: read-only consumption of an existing coverage artifact should be the default, and any execution path needs an explicit trust model and opt-in.

findings.title: The architecture does not state how normalized review findings are keyed to a commit reliably
findings.description: The ingest step is to tie findings to “project, commit and slice where known.” The existing review artifact does stamp `reviewedSha` when git is available (`src/squadron/review/persistence.py` omits the key entirely when it cannot be resolved), and the review’s own target contributes `slice:`/`pr:` frontmatter. The architecture does not say what happens when `reviewedSha` is absent, nor whether the finding is then project-level only, nor whether a code review of a diff — not the whole commit — is being compared against a whole-tree snapshot. A review scoped to a diff measures findings in changed code, while a snapshot measures whole-repository state; joining them without saying so produces misleading before/after claims. The scope dimension (diff range vs whole tree) needs to be part of the finding record and the report comparison.

findings.title: The document’s “no change to the tech-debt-audit skill” boundary conflicts with the three-copy vocabulary requirement it introduces
findings.description: The Non-Goals forbid changing the tech-debt-audit skill, but the write-time categorization discussion acknowledges that the vocabulary will then exist in three places — the Python enum, the audit skill file, and the review templates — with 323’s sync test extended to cover the third. The skill is a vendored fork whose canonical home is the external `github:ecorkran/tech-debt-audit` repository, and 323 explicitly established fork → vendored copy → installed copies as the sync direction. Adding review-template copies to that sync set means a category addition can no longer be landed only in squadron; it must go to the external fork and be re-vendored, or the “no change” boundary is violated. The document should state the canonical-source and sync direction for the expanded vocabulary rather than describing the duplication and its test mitigation without resolving ownership.

findings.title: The static-snapshot and review-normalization scopes are oversized relative to the stated deliverable
findings.description: Five slices are proposed, of which one covers an entire language adapter with complexity, duplication, file-length, function-length, lint counts, type-error counts, coverage, exclusions, rule-set identity, and project-declared limits. That is a multi-engine subsystem with no language-independent tool backing all of it — the document itself notes type errors and complexity have no language-agnostic solution. The architecture also names 420 and 440 as consumers, but their stated needs are narrower: 420 wants lint/type/test signals and normalized review findings for scoring; 440 wants a baseline it can offer. The duplication metric and automatic coverage execution are the most deferrable pieces: they add tool-selection and environment complexity without being required by either named consumer. Cut duplication and coverage from the first release, keep complexity/length/lint/type-error for one language, and let additional metrics be added only when a named consumer needs them; that reduces the keystone to a record contract, one adapter, and a report that is actually implementable.
